prompt: A 30,000-bit message crosses three store-and-forward links in a row, each 10 Mbit/s, with negligible propagation and processing delay. How long does it take to arrive if it is sent (a) as one 30,000-bit packet and (b) as three 10,000-bit packets? Ignore per-packet header overhead and assume initially idle links with no other traffic.

options.explanation: That's the time to cross *one* link. Store-and-forward means each router must receive a packet fully before sending it on, so the transmission time is paid per link.
Correct for (a), but (b) is faster: while packet 2 is being sent on link 1, packet 1 is already moving on link 2. The links work in parallel.
Correct. One big packet: 3 links × 3 ms = 9 ms. Three small packets pipeline: the first needs 3 ms to cross three links, and each of the other two arrives 1 ms after the one before, so 5 ms.
This assumes the three packets can travel fully in parallel. Each still needs 1 ms per link, and the last packet can't start until the first two have gone out on link 1.

workedExample:
**(a) One 30,000-bit packet.** Each link must transmit the whole packet before the next can start:

```formula
d_trans = 30,000 bit / (10⁷ bit/s)
d_trans = 3 ms
T_a = 3 × d_trans = 9 ms
where
d_trans: the transmission delay of one packet on one 10 Mbit/s (10⁷ bits per second) link
bit: one binary digit; bit/s is bits per second
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
T_a: the total time for the single packet over three store-and-forward links
In words: the 3 ms transmission is paid three times in a row, giving **9 ms**.
```

**(b) Three 10,000-bit packets.** Each transmission takes 1 ms. Timeline (ms):

```
time     L1   L2   L3
0-1 ms   P1
1-2 ms   P2   P1
2-3 ms   P3   P2   P1
3-4 ms        P3   P2
4-5 ms             P3
```

Last bit arrives at **5 ms**. In general:

```formula
T = (N + P − 1) × L / R
T = (3 + 3 − 1) × 1 ms = 5 ms
where
T: the time until the last packet has fully arrived
N: the number of store-and-forward links, 3
P: the number of equal-sized packets, 3
L: the length of each packet, in bits (10,000)
R: the link rate, in bits per second (10⁷); L / R is 1 ms
ms: milliseconds
In words: the first packet takes N transmission times to cross the links, and each further packet arrives one transmission time after the one before it.
```

This pipelining effect is one reason networks split data into packets rather than sending whole messages. (Each packet also needs headers, so splitting too finely backfires.)
